![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14080406/assets/e8a9dfb3ff189e96089c73ead8a3b44f04aa1684894c44203afb8884ad75c9e1.png)

For the function $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2$ shown above, what is the expression for the area $A$ as a definite integral?
questions.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between the function $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=-1.5$ and $x=0.5.$

This can be expressed as the definite integral of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2$ between the lower limit $x=-1.5$ and the upper limit $x=0.5,$ as follows:

$$
A={\int }_{-1.5}^{0.5}(-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum
questions.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0,$ and the upper bound is $b=1.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{1-0}{n}=\frac{1}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(0+i\cdot \frac{1}{n})\,\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(\frac{i}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{i}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{4}2{x}^{-4}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{l}=a+lΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}2{x}^{-4}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=2{x}^{-4},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-(1)}{n}=\frac{3}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}2{x}^{-4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+l\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{3l}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[2{(1+\frac{3l}{n})}^{-4}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{6}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=2$ and the upper bound is $b=6.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{6-2}{n}=\frac{4}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{6}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[f(2+j\cdot \frac{4}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[f(2+\frac{4j}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+\frac{4j}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}9{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=9{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14080406/assets/f02616ea8f44865a727bec3affe596503dbadacafb113acad6e5f755218b4ff5.png)

For the function $y = -2x^3+2$ shown above, write down an expression for the area $\mathcal{A}$ as a definite integral.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $\mathcal{A}$ between the function $f(x) = -2x^3+2$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=0$ and $x=1.$

This can be expressed as the definite integral of $f(x) = -2x^3+2$ between the lower limit $x=0$ and the upper limit $x=1,$ as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \mathcal{A} = \int_0^1 (-2x^3+2)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum
canonical_examples.problem: Express $\displaystyle \int_1^3(4-x)\,\textrm{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k)\Delta x,
$$

    

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

In the definite integral

$$
\displaystyle \int_1^3(4-x)\,\textrm{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x) = 4-x,$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{3-1}{n} = \dfrac 2 n,
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}(4-x)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\,Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(1+k\cdot \frac{2}{n})\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{2k}{n})\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[(4-(1+\frac{2k}{n}))\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[(3-\frac{2k}{n})\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that $\displaystyle \int_{3}^b f(x)\, \textrm d x =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left[\left(3 + \dfrac{5k}{n}\right)^2\cdot \dfrac 5 n\right].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
\int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f\left(x_k\right)\cdot \Delta x
$$

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a = 3.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $\Delta x = \dfrac{5}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\dfrac{5}{n} = \dfrac{b-3}{n} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad b = 8.
$$

Consequently, $x_k = 3 + \dfrac{5k}{n}$ and $f(x_k) = x_{k}^2.$

Hence,

$$
\int_{3}^{8} x^2 \, \textrm d x =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left[\left(3 + \dfrac{5k}{n}\right)^2\cdot \dfrac 5 n\right].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)= x^2$ and $b = 8.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum
canonical_examples.problem: Express $\displaystyle \int_1^2 x^2\,\textrm d x$ as the limit of a right Riemann sum.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,\textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n f(x_k)\cdot\Delta x,
$$

where $x_k = a + k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x =  \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
\displaystyle \int_1^2 x^2\,\textrm d x,
$$

the function is $f(x) = x^2,$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{2-1}{n} = \dfrac 1 n.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\,Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+k\cdot \frac{1}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+\frac{k}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[{(1+\frac{k}{n})}^{2}\,\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$
